_meta.name: BankSploit CTF vulnerability configuration
_meta.description: Per-vulnerability training levels. level 0 = fully vulnerable, 1 = weak mitigation, 2 = partial fix, 3 = secure. isVulnerable() is true while level < 3. ctf_active marks whether a vulnerability is included in the current CTF event (managed on the CTF Vulnerabilities page). ctf_eligible = false marks a vulnerability as training/pentest-only: it still appears in the labs with its full level ladder, but can never be selected into a CTF, scored, or delivered a flag (absent key = eligible).
_meta.id_scheme: Keys within each module are the spec IDs lowercased (g1..g12, l1..l24). G = generic web vuln, L = banking logical vuln.
_meta.scoring: points[level] = score for capturing the flag at that level. Higher level = more mitigation bypassed = more points. Level 3 is secure (no flag, 0 points). Direction chosen 2026-11-05: reward skill.

g1.title: SQL injection (login bypass)
g1.description: Login query concatenates customer_id/password and compares the insecure password_md5 column. Also governs md5-vs-bcrypt: at level 3 the query is parameterized and uses password_verify() against password_hash.
g1.attack_scenario: Login as any user with ' OR 1=1 -- in customer_id. At level 1 a basic blacklist blocks OR but not UNION.
hints: The login form sends your input straight into a query. What happens if your Customer ID contains a single quote?
Comment out the password check. MySQL's -- comment needs a trailing space; the query is one line.
Try Customer ID: ADMIN001' --  (trailing space), any password. At level 1, OR is filtered — pivot to a UNION SELECT.

l10.title: OTP brute-force
l10.description: 4-digit OTP (login/transfer) valid for 24h with no rate limiting and no lockout. Secondary module: transfer.
l10.attack_scenario: Only 10,000 combinations and the code stays valid for 24h — at ~500 req/s any OTP falls in seconds.
hints: The OTP is only 4 digits. Is anything stopping you from trying again?
Check for rate limiting / lockout after failed OTP attempts — there is none at level 0.
Script 0000–9999 against the verify endpoint; no counter increments failed_attempts for OTP.

l11.title: OTP in response body
l11.description: The /auth/login JSON response includes the generated OTP 'for dev convenience' and it was never removed.
l11.attack_scenario: Read the OTP straight from the login API response — no SMS access needed.
hints: You don't have the victim's phone. Do you even need it?
Inspect the full JSON returned by the login call.
The otp field is present in the response body at level 0; use it directly.

l12.title: JWT alg:none
l12.description: Login issues a JWT. At level 0 the verifier accepts alg=none (unsigned), allowing forgery without the secret. At level 3 only HS256 with the server secret is accepted.
l12.attack_scenario: Forge a token with header {"alg":"none"} and arbitrary claims to bypass authentication.
hints: Decode the JWT (base64url). Look at the header's alg field.
What if you set alg to none and drop the signature?
Re-encode header {"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"} with a forged payload and empty signature; the server trusts it at level 0.

l13.title: Predictable reset tokens
l13.description: Password reset tokens are sequential integers or base64(user_id + timestamp), not random.
l13.attack_scenario: Guess another user's reset token and take over the account.
hints: Request a reset and look closely at the token — is it random?
Try decoding it; is it base64 of predictable values?
Increment/derive the token for another user_id and submit it to the reset endpoint.

l16.title: Account enumeration
l16.description: Distinct messages: 'Customer ID not found' vs 'Incorrect password'; register/forgot-password leak existence too.
l16.attack_scenario: Enumerate valid Customer IDs / emails from differing responses.
hints: Compare the error for a bad Customer ID vs a good ID with a bad password.
Different messages = an oracle for which accounts exist.
At level 3 the message is identical regardless of which part was wrong.

l14.title: Session fixation
l14.description: The session id is not regenerated on login at level 0, so a pre-set session id remains valid after authentication.
l14.attack_scenario: Fix a victim's session id before they log in, then reuse it to ride their authenticated session.
hints: Does the session cookie change value after you log in?
Set a known session id, log in, and check if it still works.
Level 3 calls session_regenerate_id() on login.

l17.title: PII embedded in JWT
l17.description: At vuln levels the JWT payload carries PAN, masked Aadhaar and account balance in plaintext (base64url, not encrypted).
l17.attack_scenario: Decode the JWT payload to read the user's PAN/Aadhaar/balance without any further access.
hints: A JWT payload is only base64url-encoded, not encrypted.
Decode the middle segment of your token.
Level 3 keeps sensitive fields out of the token.

l25.title: Session puzzling
l25.description: The password-reset flow overloads the same session key used for authentication, so completing step 1 can grant an authenticated session (email-only account takeover).
l25.attack_scenario: Drive the reset flow so the shared session key authenticates you without the password step.
hints: The reset flow and login write the same session key.
What state does step 1 of the reset leave in your session?
Level 3 uses a separate, namespaced key for the reset flow.

g2.title: SQL injection (data extraction)
g2.description: The Statements SEARCH box only (remarks filter) concatenates input; the date range is always bound. Graduated via g2_term(): L0 raw -> in-band UNION or error-based extraction (raw SQL error shown); L1 leaky single-pass blacklist strips union/select and comment tokens with raw errors still shown (bypass by nesting keywords and balancing the quote, then UNION or error-based); L2 strips UNION repeatedly with errors hidden, so only boolean-blind extraction remains; L3 parameterized (g2_is_secure()). The target is each user's per-user flag in the ctf_flags table (columns flag + username).
g2.attack_scenario: L0: %' UNION SELECT username,flag,3,4,5,6,7 FROM ctf_flags-- (7 columns; flag goes in the Remarks cell because the Date cell is truncated to 10 chars), or error-based via extractvalue(). L1: nest keywords (UNIunionON SELselectECT) and end with ' OR '%'='. L2: boolean-blind, e.g. house%' AND SUBSTRING((SELECT flag FROM ctf_flags WHERE username='<you>'),1,1)='B'-- , one character at a time.
hints: Only the search (remarks) box is injectable — it is spliced into remarks LIKE '%...%'. The query returns 7 columns; the flag lives in ctf_flags (flag + username).

L0: UNION SELECT username,flag,... FROM ctf_flags — flag shows in the Remarks cell (the Date cell is truncated to 10 chars); or extractvalue() error-based. L1: the filter strips union/select + comments in one pass — nest them (UNIunionON) and balance the quote since comments are gone.
L2: UNION is stripped repeatedly and errors are hidden, so go boolean-blind — use your rows appearing/vanishing as the oracle and read the flag one character at a time (SUBSTRING + AND).

g4.title: Reflected XSS
g4.description: Training/pentest only (ctf_eligible = false): reflected XSS shown with its full mitigation ladder, not part of the CTF and never scored. The Statements search term is reflected into the page in two contexts — body text and the search box value="..." attribute. Graduated via g4_text()/g4_attr(): L0 raw text reflection (/
g4.attack_scenario: ?q= executes in your own browser (reflected). At L1 use an event handler or a nested
hints: Your search term is reflected back on the results page and into the search box value attribute.
Craft a payload that executes in your browser — an or
At L2 the body text is encoded but the value="..." attribute is raw — break out with ">. At L3 both contexts are encoded and nothing runs.

g9.title: Command injection
g9.description: The PDF 'Download' control shells out (wkhtmltopdf) with the user-supplied output filename concatenated into the command line unescaped, so shell metacharacters in ?filename= run OS commands. A graduated blacklist ladder hardens the filter, but every blacklist is incomplete. L0: no filter (stmt.pdf;cat /tmp/flag_g9_<uid>.txt;). L1: strips ; and & — use a pipe instead (stmt.pdf|cat /tmp/flag_g9_<uid>.txt). L2: also strips | and spaces — separate with a newline (%0a) and use $IFS for spaces (stmt.pdf%0acat$IFS/tmp/flag_g9_<uid>.txt). L3 escapeshellarg()s every argument and blocks all of it. Commands run in an emulated honeypot shell (no real execution, no network egress); the flag is the per-user file flag_g9_<uid>.txt — find its exact name with ls /tmp.
g9.attack_scenario: Inject a second command through ?filename= on Download PDF and read the per-user flag file. Each level removes the previous separator, so escalate the metacharacter: ; (L0) -> | pipe (L1) -> newline + $IFS (L2). Discover the flag file name with ls /tmp, then cat /tmp/flag_g9_<uid>.txt.
hints: The PDF output filename (?filename=) is concatenated into the command unescaped. Chain a command with ';': filename=stmt.pdf;id; proves RCE, filename=stmt.pdf;ls /tmp; reveals flag_g9_<uid>.txt, then cat it.
L1 strips ';' and '&' from the filename, so stmt.pdf;cat... collapses into one token. Use a separator that survives: a pipe. filename=stmt.pdf|cat /tmp/flag_g9_<uid>.txt.

L2 also strips '|' and spaces. Separate commands with a newline (%0a) and replace spaces with $IFS: filename=stmt.pdf%0acat$IFS/tmp/flag_g9_<uid>.txt. Other space-less tricks also work: ${IFS}, $IFS$9 (an empty positional param), a literal tab (%09, which the filter forgets), or brace expansion {cat,/tmp/flag_g9_<uid>.txt}. L3 escapes every argument and blocks all of these.

l1.title: IDOR — View Other Accounts' Statements
l1.description: The account_number parameter in the statements URL is resolved without ownership check. Changing it to another user's account number exposes their transactions.
l1.attack_scenario: Discover other account numbers from the beneficiaries page, then change ?account= in the Statements URL to view their transactions.
hints: Look at the URL when viewing your statements. What identifies the account?
Where else in the app can you see other account numbers?
Level 3 verifies the account belongs to the logged-in user before loading transactions.

g8.title: Path traversal (CSV export)
g8.description: The CSV export ?file= parameter is concatenated into a path with no sanitisation, so ../ sequences read arbitrary files.
g8.attack_scenario: Set ?file=../../../../etc/passwd (or any path) on the export endpoint to stream arbitrary files.
hints: The export lets you name a file. Where is that path rooted?
Try climbing out of the export directory with ../
Level 3 uses basename() and confines the path to the export dir with a .csv suffix.

l1.title: IDOR — Transfer from Other Account
l1.description: The transfer form sends the source account as a from_account_ref value and the server debits it without checking ownership, so you can transfer out of any account. A graduated ladder hardens how that reference is protected, but each protection is client-side and defeatable with only the browser and its DevTools (no tools, no endpoint guessing). L0 posts the raw account number. At L1 the client sends the plain number AND its HMAC signature (from_account_ref + from_account_sig); the server verifies hash_hmac(number)==sig in O(1) but never checks ownership. Editing just the number leaves the signature empty/mismatched so the naive tamper is rejected — but valid number->signature pairs for accounts you don't own leak in the page JS (a dstSig/payee map, kept in a separate block from the srcSig map of your own accounts), and replaying a victim's pair is accepted as the source. L2 posts AES ciphertext whose key/IV/algorithm ship to the browser in transfer-ref.js, so you extract the key and forge the victim's ciphertext. L3 verifies ownership and blocks all of it.
l1.attack_scenario: Change the From-account reference to another user's account so the transfer debits their balance: at L0 edit the option value to the victim's number; at L1 watch the Network request (from_account_ref=number + from_account_sig=hmac), find the signatures in the page JS, locate the separate payee map (dstSig) that leaks the victim's number->signature pair, and submit the victim's number with its matching signature; at L2 read transfer-ref.js for the AES key and run XferRef.encryptRef('<victim>') in the console, then submit the ciphertext.
hints: The From account is posted as from_account_ref. At L0 that value is just the account number — edit the <select> option in DevTools to another account's number.

At L1 the form sends the plain number AND a signature (from_account_ref + from_account_sig); editing only the number fails because the server recomputes HMAC(number) and compares. Search the page JS: a srcSig map holds your accounts' number->signature pairs, and a separate dstSig/payee map leaks valid pairs for accounts you don't own. Submit a victim's number with ITS signature (set fromRef and fromSig from dstSig) and the server accepts it. You cannot forge signatures (secret is server-side), only reuse leaked pairs.

At L2 the dropdown shows plain numbers, but a page script encrypts your selected account with XferRef.encryptRef() and posts the AES ciphertext in the hidden from_account_ref. Editing the <select> to a victim's number isn't on the page's own-account allowlist, so it posts empty and is rejected — you must forge the ciphertext yourself. The key, IV and algorithm ship to the browser in /public/vendor/transfer-ref.js: read it, run XferRef.encryptRef('<victim number>') in the console (or the equivalent CryptoJS.AES.encrypt), set #fromRef to the result and submit. L3 verifies the account's user_id matches the session user and blocks all of these.

g5.title: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)
g5.description: State-changing transfer requests do not validate a CSRF token at vuln levels, so a forged cross-site form can move money. Governed together with the wizard (transfer.l9) via the core CSRF class.
g5.attack_scenario: Host a page that auto-submits a transfer form to the victim's session; no token is checked.
hints: Does the transfer form carry an unpredictable token the server checks?
Build an external form that POSTs a transfer.
Level 3 validates a per-session CSRF token on every state change.

l2.title: IDOR — transfer receipt
l2.description: The transfer receipt endpoint returns any receipt by id with no ownership check.
l2.attack_scenario: Increment or change the receipt id in the URL to read other users' transfer receipts.
hints: Receipts are addressed by id. Is that id tied to you?
Change the receipt id in the request.
Level 3 verifies the receipt belongs to the logged-in user.

l6.title: Negative-amount transfer
l6.description: The transfer amount is not checked for amount > 0, so a negative amount reverses the flow and credits the attacker.
l6.attack_scenario: Submit a transfer with a negative amount to pull money from the destination into your account.
hints: What happens if the amount is less than zero?
The server trusts the sign of the amount.
Level 3 rejects non-positive amounts.

l7.title: Race condition / double-spend
l7.description: Balance read-check-write is not atomic and takes no row lock, so concurrent transfers can overdraw the account.
l7.attack_scenario: Fire many identical transfers in parallel to spend the same balance more than once.
hints: The balance is read, checked, then written — not in one step.
Send concurrent requests before the first one commits.
Level 3 uses an atomic update / row lock.

l9.title: Wizard step-skipping / OTP skip
l9.description: The transfer /execute stage runs with no check that earlier wizard stages completed, and an absent otp field skips OTP verification.
l9.attack_scenario: POST directly to the execute stage, omitting the OTP step, to complete a transfer without verification.
hints: The transfer is a multi-step wizard. Must the steps run in order?
Call the final stage directly.
Level 3 enforces the state machine and a mandatory OTP.

l20.title: Rounding / salami
l20.description: Interest accrual uses lossy floating-point math, so fractional remainders can be skimmed over many operations.
l20.attack_scenario: Exploit floating-point rounding in interest to accumulate fractions of currency.
hints: How is interest calculated — integer paise or floating point?
Rounding leaves tiny remainders each time.
Level 3 uses integer/decimal math.

l21.title: Daily-limit bypass
l21.description: Only the per-transaction amount is checked against the daily limit, so splitting a large transfer into several bypasses it.
l21.attack_scenario: Split an over-limit transfer into multiple under-limit transfers in the same day.
hints: The limit is checked per transaction, not per day.
Make several smaller transfers.
Level 3 tracks the cumulative daily total.

l23.title: Self-transfer cashback abuse
l23.description: Self-transfers (destination owned by the sender) still earn the 1% cashback, so money moved between own accounts mints rewards.
l23.attack_scenario: Repeatedly transfer between your own accounts to farm cashback.
hints: Who is the destination allowed to be?
Does cashback apply when you pay yourself?
Level 3 excludes self-transfers from cashback.

g3.title: Stored XSS (beneficiary name)
g3.description: The biller/beneficiary name is stored raw and later rendered unescaped, so stored HTML/JS executes for anyone who views it.
g3.attack_scenario: Save a beneficiary whose name contains a <script> payload; it runs when the list renders.
hints: The beneficiary name is shown back on later pages.
Is it encoded when stored or displayed?
Level 3 escapes the name on output with htmlspecialchars().

l3.title: IDOR — beneficiary id
l3.description: Beneficiary fetch/delete acts on any id with no ownership check.
l3.attack_scenario: Change the beneficiary id to view or delete another user's payees.
hints: Beneficiaries are addressed by id. Is the id scoped to you?
Change the id in the request.
Level 3 checks the beneficiary belongs to the current user.

l8.title: Cooling-period bypass
l8.description: The new-beneficiary cooling period is enforced using a client-supplied timestamp, so the client can backdate it.
l8.attack_scenario: Set the client timestamp into the past to send to a freshly added beneficiary immediately.
hints: Who decides when the beneficiary was added?
The cooling check trusts a value you send.
Level 3 uses the server time stored at creation.

g6.title: Server-side request forgery (SSRF)
g6.description: The loan document-URL fetch retrieves any client-supplied URL with no allow-list, reaching internal hosts and cloud metadata.
g6.attack_scenario: Supply a document URL pointing at an internal service or 169.254.169.254 metadata endpoint.
hints: The server fetches a URL you provide.
Point it at an internal/link-local address.
Level 3 allows only https hosts on an allow-list and blocks private ranges.

g7.title: Unrestricted file upload
g7.description: KYC document upload performs no server-side validation at level 0, so any extension (e.g. .php) is written to the web-served uploads directory — a webshell.
g7.attack_scenario: Upload a .php file and browse to it under /uploads to get code execution.
hints: What file types does the upload actually accept?
Try a .php file instead of an image.
Level 3 validates extension + MIME and stores outside the web root.

g10.title: XML external entity (XXE)
g10.description: The loan XML import enables external entities (LIBXML_NOENT | LIBXML_DTDLOAD), so a crafted DOCTYPE reads local files.
g10.attack_scenario: Import XML with an external entity referencing file:///etc/passwd to exfiltrate file contents.
hints: The XML import resolves entities.
Declare a DOCTYPE with an external SYSTEM entity.
Level 3 disables entity loading and network access in the parser.

l22.title: Loan parameter tampering
l22.description: Loan application parameters (amount, rate, tenure) are trusted from the request without server-side bounds, so the applicant sets favourable terms.
l22.attack_scenario: Tamper the interest rate or amount in the loan application request.
hints: Which loan terms come from the form vs the server?
Change the rate or amount in the request.
Level 3 derives and validates terms server-side.

l24.title: Card data in plaintext
l24.description: The cards API returns full PAN and CVV in plaintext with no ownership check. This one dial also governs block/unblock IDOR (CWE-639), a broken PIN change that does not require the old PIN (CWE-620), and spending-limit mass assignment (CWE-915).
l24.attack_scenario: Call the cards API for any card id to read PAN/CVV, block cards you do not own, or change limits/PIN.
hints: What does the card detail API return, and for whose cards?
Try another card id.
Level 3 encrypts/masks card data and checks ownership on every card action.

l5.title: Mass assignment + IDOR
l5.description: Profile update writes request fields verbatim, so role and is_locked are bindable, and the target user_id/id is taken from the request (IDOR).
l5.attack_scenario: Add role=admin (or a different user_id) to the profile update to escalate or edit another user.
hints: Which fields does the profile update accept?
Try sending role or is_locked, or another user_id.
Level 3 whitelists editable fields and scopes the update to the session user.

l4.title: Broken function-level authorization
l4.description: Admin surfaces are gated by login only at vuln levels; level 1 trusts a spoofable client signal (X-Admin header / is_admin cookie). Real role checks happen only at level 3.
l4.attack_scenario: Access admin endpoints as a normal user, or send X-Admin: true / is_admin=true at level 1.
hints: Are admin pages checking your role, or just that you are logged in?
Look for a client-controlled admin signal.
Level 3 enforces a genuine server-side role check on every admin surface.

l19.title: Hidden API fields
l19.description: Account/user API responses include internal-only columns (role, password_md5, last_login_ip, …) that should never be exposed.
l19.attack_scenario: Read internal fields straight from the account/whoami API response.
hints: Look at every field the account API returns.
Some columns are internal-only.
Level 3 returns an explicit whitelist of safe fields.

l18.title: Information disclosure
l18.description: Verbose errors leak messages/stack traces, and forgotten debug endpoints (/api/v1/debug/config, /phpinfo, /whoami) dump DB credentials, the JWT secret and full environment.
l18.attack_scenario: Hit the debug endpoints or trigger an error to read secrets and internals.
hints: Uncaught errors may print more than they should.
Look for leftover /debug endpoints.
Level 3 shows generic errors and removes the debug routes.

g12.title: Insecure deserialization
g12.description: The bs_prefs cookie is base64(PHP serialize(...)) and unserialize() runs on it, enabling PHP object injection via a gadget (PrefLogger writes attacker content to an attacker path on destruct).
g12.attack_scenario: Craft a serialized PrefLogger object in the bs_prefs cookie to write a file (e.g. a webshell).
hints: How are your preferences stored in the cookie?
unserialize() on attacker input can instantiate objects.
Level 3 uses JSON only, which cannot instantiate objects.

g11.title: Local file inclusion
g11.description: The help-page ?page parameter is concatenated into include() with no validation; wrappers and traversal read or execute arbitrary content.
hints: The help viewer includes a file named by ?page.
Try traversal or a php:// filter wrapper.
Level 1 strips ../ (bypass with ....//); level 3 uses a strict whitelist with no dynamic include.
